name: Gynecomastia surgery

card.summary: Surgical removal of excess glandular and fatty chest tissue in men; the established medical route when enlargement persists, with documented complication risks and variable insurance coverage.
card.aka: Male breast reduction, gynecomastia correction, subcutaneous mastectomy
card.note: Surgical procedure with documented complications such as hematoma, asymmetry and altered sensation; often classed as cosmetic by insurers.

quick.overview:
Gynecomastia is enlargement of glandular breast tissue in males. Surgery removes that tissue, often combined with liposuction of surrounding fat, to flatten the chest contour. Reference sources describe it as the main treatment when the condition persists beyond about a year, is distressing, and has become fibrotic.

In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a chest-contouring procedure, and clinical studies have examined its effect on quality of life, particularly in adolescents and young men.
quick.mechanism: Techniques described in the literature include subcutaneous mastectomy through a small incision around the areola, liposuction-assisted removal, and laser-assisted variants. The aim is to remove glandular tissue, which liposuction alone may not address.
quick.risks: Reported complications include hematoma, infection, seroma, asymmetry, altered nipple or breast sensation, visible scarring, contour irregularities and, rarely, nipple or areola necrosis. Many US insurers classify the procedure as cosmetic and deny coverage. Pubertal gynecomastia often resolves on its own, so surgery in teenagers is generally deferred.

lead: Gynecomastia surgery, also called male breast reduction, is a set of operations that remove excess glandular tissue and, often, fat from the male chest, producing a flatter, more masculine chest contour.[1] Gynecomastia itself results from an altered balance between estrogen and androgen activity and can arise during puberty, in older age, with certain medications or illnesses, or without an identified cause.[1] For many men the operation is the way to change chest shape that diet, training and fat loss do not alter.

Reference sources describe surgery as considered when enlargement has persisted for roughly a year or more, causes physical or psychological distress, and has become fibrotic, and as typically reserved for cases that do not respond to medication.[1] The American Board of Cosmetic Surgery, cited on Wikipedia, calls surgery the most effective known treatment for the condition.[1] In 2019 about 24,000 men in the US had the procedure, 19 percent more than in 2000, and about 60 percent were under 29.[1]

Published work on the operation consists largely of observational series, database analyses, technique comparisons and quality-of-life questionnaires, plus a number of small registered trials of specific methods.[3][4][5]

paras: True gynecomastia involves growth of glandular breast tissue; pseudogynecomastia is enlargement from excess fat or skin without glandular tissue and is commonly associated with obesity, and a physical examination can distinguish the two.[1] Surgery centres on removing glandular tissue, with liposuction used for the fatty component.[1][8] Gynecomastia is common in adolescence: up to 65 percent of adolescent boys may develop it, usually peaking around ages 13 to 14, and it is self-limited in 75 to 90 percent, resolving within one to three years, though about 10 percent still have it at 17.[1]

Pubertal gynecomastia is common and usually regresses within one to three years, and reference sources note that surgery is generally postponed until puberty is complete [1]. A study of adolescents who underwent surgery at a Korean hospital notes that most adolescent cases resolve spontaneously within about three years, while persistent cases can affect psychological development [6]. Wikipedia notes surgery is generally reserved for chronic cases that do not respond to medication, and that adolescent surgery should wait until puberty is complete (Tanner stage V).[1]

In adults, persistent gynecomastia may follow medication effects, chronic illness, or hormone therapy. In men treated with hormone therapy for prostate cancer, large randomized studies reported gynecomastia in around half or more of patients, and it was cited as a leading reason for stopping therapy early [7]. Tissue removed during surgery is routinely sent for pathology, though its usefulness in adolescents has been questioned because breast cancer is rare in that group [1].

Described approaches include subcutaneous mastectomy, liposuction-assisted mastectomy, laser-assisted liposuction and laser-lipolysis without suction [1]. A systematic review has examined liposuction-assisted surgery through a minimal periareolar incision [8]. Registered trials have compared endoscopic and open surgery, periareolar excision versus a pull-through technique, modified Benelli procedures, and laparoscopic gland resection combined with nipple-areola complex lift [9][10][11][12][13]. A trial has also tested a radiofrequency-assisted device as an adjunct in gynecomastia surgery [14]. The systematic review of liposuction-assisted surgery through a minimal incision identified 18 eligible studies out of 415 covering 1,628 patients with an average age of about 23; liposuction was described as easing removal through a small incision and consistently improving satisfaction, but complication rates ranged from 0.06 to 26.67 percent, reoperation rates from 0.6 to 25 percent, and only two studies of 25 patients rated as good quality.[8]

Published reports on recovery are procedure-specific. Trials of different methods have measured anaesthesia approach, drain use and bleeding control, including a pectoral plane block versus an erector spinae plane block and different applications of tranexamic acid.[16][17] A paper on drains evaluated the necessity of suction drains in gynecomastia surgery.[18] Quality-of-life outcomes are covered under clinical studies.

A prospective case-control study of 50 male patients (mean age about 25) used the SF-36 health questionnaire before and after surgery to assess quality of life and satisfaction.[4] A later study examined complications and quality of life after correction in adolescents and young men.[5] A national multi-institutional database analysis reviewed outcomes and complication rates in 204 pediatric and 1,583 adult cases.[3]

A study at a Korean hospital, where 71 of 1,454 gynecomastia surgery patients between January 2014 and May 2016 were adolescents, described characteristics and short-term outcomes in teenagers, noting that persistent gynecomastia can affect psychoemotional development.[6] In men treated with hormone therapy for prostate cancer, large randomised studies reported gynecomastia in around half or more of patients.[7]

A review of US insurance policies (61 companies including Medicare) found 38 percent had no well-defined gynecomastia policy and assessed requests case by case, while the 62 percent with a policy often required documentation of breast size, BMI, symptom duration and prior treatments, with requirements varying between insurers.[15] Registered trials include comparisons of endoscopic and open surgery, periareolar excision versus pull-through, modified Benelli procedures, and a radiofrequency-assisted adjunct.[9][10][11][14]

Reference sources list hematoma, wound infection, seroma, asymmetry, altered breast sensation, necrosis of the nipple or areola, visible or painful scarring and contour deformities as possible complications [1]. Large database analyses report complication rates for both adult and pediatric patients [3].

Many US insurers treat gynecomastia surgery as cosmetic and deny coverage, and published reviews have compared the criteria that insurers use.[1][15] In 2019 the average surgeon's fee was about $4,123, making it the 11th most costly male cosmetic surgery that year.[1] In looksmaxxing and hardmaxxing communities it is discussed as one of the standard surgical options for chest appearance. On T Nation, users in a long-running thread told a poster with a chest lump that surgery would be needed and that fat loss would only reduce its size, and a teenager described feeling self-conscious about mild gynecomastia and puffy nipples.[19][20]

timeline.event: About 24,000 US men have gynecomastia surgery, 19 percent more than in 2000; average surgeon fee about $4,100.[1]

lore.intro: Gynecomastia is discussed on training and looks forums mainly as a chest-appearance problem, with surgery named as the definitive option.[19][20]

claims.claim: Fat loss alone will not remove a true glandular lump; surgery is needed
claims.believers: Forum users say losing fat reduces the size of the lump but not the glandular tissue underneath, so surgery is the fix.[19]
claims.experts: Reference sources distinguish pseudogynecomastia (fat) from true gynecomastia (glandular tissue), and describe surgery as the most effective known treatment for persistent, fibrotic cases.[1]

claims.claim: Mild gynecomastia in teenagers often goes away by itself
claims.believers: Users who had it as teens say it improved with time and training.[20]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports it is self-limited in 75 to 90 percent of adolescents within one to three years, with surgery generally postponed until puberty is complete.[1][6]

angle.text: Gynecomastia surgery removes the glandular tissue and fat that give the male chest a rounded or puffy shape, and the change is visible once swelling settles. People use it when the chest has not responded to fat loss or training.
